content: Desmocollin-3 (DSC3) is a protein encoded by the DSC3 gene in humans. Members of the desmosomal family, including DSC3, are organized into two clusters on chromosome 18, occupying a combined region of less than 650 kilobases. Alternative splicing of the DSC3 gene results in two transcript variants that encode distinct isoforms. Desmocollin-3 is a calcium-dependent glycoprotein and a member of the desmocollin subfamily within the cadherin superfamily. Desmosomal proteins, including desmocollins and desmogleins, are predominantly found in epithelial cells. These proteins are essential components of desmosomes, which are specialized cell-cell junctions that mediate adhesion between cells and are critical for the structural integrity of tissues. The absence of these components disrupts cell adhesion and increases cellular motility. In the context of breast cancer, the expression of Desmocollin-3 is frequently downregulated due to epigenetic silencing mechanisms. A hereditary condition known as hereditary hypotrichosis has been associated with mutations in the DSC3 gene. In one consanguineous Afghan family, three sisters aged 12 to 18 years and their 5-year-old brother exhibited features of hereditary hypotrichosis, which included sparse scalp hair and recurrent vesicles on the scalp and skin. At birth, scalp hair was present, but after ritual shaving at one week of age, the regrown hair was fragile and began falling out by 2 to 3 months of age, eventually leaving only sparse hair on the scalp. Vesicles, less than 1 cm in diameter, were observed on the scalp and skin across most of the body. These vesicles intermittently disappeared and reappeared, sometimes rupturing and releasing fluid, which left scars that took 3 to 4 months to heal. No mucosal vesicles were observed. Affected individuals also lacked eyebrows, eyelashes, axillary hair, and body hair. However, their teeth, nails, palms, soles, sweating, hearing, and electrocardiography results were normal. Serum levels of IgA, IgE, and IgD were measured in one individual and showed no abnormalities compared to controls. The parents of the affected individuals were clinically unaffected. A scalp biopsy from the 18-year-old sister revealed slight follicular plugging, mild perivascular and periadnexal inflammatory cell presence, and normal hair follicles. Sebaceous glands appeared morphologically normal and were connected to the hair follicles. Genetic analysis identified a homozygous 2129T-G transversion in exon 14 of the DSC3 gene in the affected family members. This mutation results in a leucine-to-termination codon substitution at position 710 (L710X), located at the junction of the transmembrane and C-terminal cytoplasmic domains. This mutation is predicted to cause premature termination of the protein, leading to nonsense-mediated decay of the mRNA or instability of the truncated protein. The unaffected parents and three healthy siblings were heterozygous for the mutation, which was not found in 100 unrelated ethnically matched controls. Desmocollin-3 has been shown to interact with plakophilin-3 (PKP3), a protein involved in desmosomal function.
